Sometimes when I’m driving over the bridge to the wholesaler, I get these sudden urges like, “What if I just turned the wheel and went over?” I don’t plan anything, but the thought pops in and scares me. I’m still running the business and taking care of the kids, but everything feels like I’m pushing through mud, tied so much to losing my dad and all the fallout since.

About a year ago, when the board decided to cut our funding and merge my department, everything started to slide. Within a couple of months of that announcement I just… deflated. I cry at work in the storage rooms over little things—labeling errors, a painting not hanging straight. I’ll be fine, and then suddenly I’m tearing up in front of a crate.

I’ve been sleeping far more than usual—10, 11 hours—and still napping on weekends. It’s not like I can’t get out of bed for days; I still make myself go in, run tours, attend meetings, but it feels heavier and slower. I’m behind on exhibition planning, and my colleagues have noticed.

I second‑guess everything now: what to wear, whether to say yes to a colleague’s invitation, even which sandwich to order. I’ll stand in my kitchen frozen over which cereal to have.

Sometimes, especially after a bad day at the museum, I’ve thought about ending it—imagining stepping in front of a late train on my commute home, picturing the platform and time of day. But those thoughts scare me; I haven’t gotten to the point of writing notes or putting anything in motion, and they seem tied to how overwhelmed I feel about the job situation rather than all the time.
